text: I now give the floor uh to her
excellency Christina Marcus Lassen, a
chair of delegation of Denmark.
Madame President,
excellencies, distinguished delegates,
a compass does not change with the
weather. It helps you find a way in fair
weather as well as in storm.
81 years ago, the world gave itself a
compass. We named it the United Nations
Charter. It has helped us stay the
course even when disease have been
anything but calm.
It has pointed us toward a world of
equal rights, self-determination of
peoples and territorial integrity of all
states, large and small towards a
rules-based international order.
The progress has been real. More than a
billion people lifted out of poverty,
standards of living transformed.
Colonial empires brought to an end.
Independent nations emerged. Peoples
gained the right to shape their own
future.
That progress was made possible because
we kept consulting the compass
because we stayed the course.
Today, it seems we are losing our way.
Wars and conflicts are at the highest
level since World War II. Extreme
poverty is under rise. Extreme weather
and climate related disasters are
hitting record highs.
Mistrust, polarization, and divisions
are growing both among states and within
societies.
Even the most basic principles of
international law, including
international humanitarian law, are
violated with impunity.
To get back on track, we must turn our
attention to the compass.
Excellencies, respect for the charter,
for human rights, for international law
is not a courtesy we extend when
convenient. These are binding
obligations we all agree to. Respecting
them is the precondition for
international peace and security.
We see this clearly in Ukraine.
Russia's illegal war of choice could end
tomorrow if Russia withdrew to his own
territory and stopped trying to redraw
borders by force. The vast majority of
UN member states and the UN Secretary
General supports calls for an immediate
and comprehensive ceasefire in Ukraine.
It is the only basis for good faith
talks aimed at a just and lasting peace
in line with international law,
including the UN charter. Ukraine has
been offering this for a year now.
Denmark's support to Ukraine will remain
steadfast. This is not only a matter of
helping Ukraine defend itself. It is a
matter of defending the universal
principles upon which this organization
was built.
Excellencies, in Sudan, the war
continues to inflict immense human
suffering. Millions are displaced.
Famine has been confirmed. And the
international community has been warned
of mass atrocities over and over again,
but has failed to act. The
responsibility for this horrific war
lies in the hand of the waring parties.
Yet, it is fueled by outside actors and
permitted by international inaction.
We must act now to prevent further mass
atrocities against the Sudin people. We
must put our political will and weight
behind a stronger demand for peace and
accountability.
The waring parties must come to the
negotiation table, engage in dialogue,
and agree to a much needed truce.
Denmarks fully support the Quint's
efforts to advance a civilian-led
political process and welcomes the
improved coordination among mediators.
Excellencies, in Syria, the fall of the
brutal asset regime offers a historic
opportunity to build a brighter future
for all Syrians. Denmark is committed to
supporting the people of Syria in a
Syrian and owned transition. It is a
glimpse of hope in a troubled region and
a stark contrast to this destabilizing
actions of Iran whose consequences are
felt far beyond the region.
Denmark's position remains clear. Iran
must never be allowed to develop or
acquire a nuclear weapon. We strongly
support continued diplomatic efforts to
restore effective international
verification of Iran's nuclear program.
And we deeply regret the unwillingness
of a few council members to acknowledge
that sanctions measures have been
reinstated in full accordance with
Security Council resolution 2231.
At the same time, we urge Iran to comply
fully with resolution 2817,
cease attacks against countries in the
region, and refrain from any actions or
threats that undermine the freedom of
navigation in the Strait of Humus.
Excellencies, last year, this assembly
endorsed the New York Declaration, a
road map toward the two-state solution,
a path to lasting peace and security for
Israelis and Palestinians.
Since then, the comprehensive plan to
end the Gaza conflict has been endorsed
by the Security Council. Now, it must be
implemented in full. We call on all
parties to stay committed to the plan.
Yet, in Gaza, civil civilians continue
to pay the price. Far more must be done
to secure humanitarian access and
long-term peace. and it the occupied
West Bank. Settler violence and
settlement expansion threatened the
daily lives of Palestinians and
undermined the prospects for a future
Palestinian state. This has to stop.
Excellencies, as an elected member of
the Security Council, Denmark strives to
ensure that the council fulfills its
mandate. At times, we succeed. This
June, the Security Council unanimously
adopted resolution 28-23
on accountability for crimes against UN
peacekeepers led by Denmark and Pakistan
and backed by a record 153 member
states. a clear signal of commitment to
the safety and security of the brave men
and women who serve under the UN flag
and a clear demonstration that the
council can still come together and
speak with one voice. Too often however
the security council is blocked by
geopolitical divisions unable to act.
Meanwhile, the cost of inaction are felt
by the civilians across the world as the
disrespect for international
humanitarian law is allowed to fester.
Excellencies, our collective inability
to halt the killings, suffering, and
injustices in Gaza, Ukraine, Sudan, and
beyond must not prompt us to surrender
to a rule world ruled by brute force. On
the contrary, it must inspire us to work
harder to sustain and strengthen the
structures, instruments, and mechanism
we have built on over the last 81 years.
To Denmark, this includes maintaining
our firm support for the ICJ and the ICC
as core international justice
institutions.
This year, Denmark nominated its first
ever candidate for judge at the ICC,
reaffirming our unwavering support for
the court at a critical time.
It also means continuing to meet the UN
target of providing 0.7% of GNI for
official development assistance. For
more than 45 years, Denmark has
consistently delivered on that goal. We
do so not as an act of altruism, but
because it's in our shared interest. It
creates jobs, opportunities, and hope
where people live, allowing them to
build a future at home, increasing
stability and mutual prosperity. We call
on fellow member states to join us
at the current juncture. However,
sustaining an order with the UN as it
core means working for reform. Reform is
how we keep this organization fit for
the world we live in. Denmark continues
to call for a fundamental security
council reform. We wish to expand the
council with more members in both
categories including permanent seat for
underrepresented regions and we wish to
commence tax-based negotiations.
Only then can we begin to redress
historical injustices.
Denmark also strongly supports the UN 80
reform process. We applaud the results
so far and call for ambitions to be
raised. We must strive to build a more
efficient and inclusive UN, a UN that
delivers better on its core mandates and
underground where it matters most. To
enable this, we call on all UN member
states to meet their financial
obligations to the UN in full and on
time.
Excellencies, let's be real. We need the
UN, not for the sake of the UN, but but
in order to address challenges that face
us all because no single country can
manage climate change, global health
threats, or the governance of emergence
technologies on its own.
The climate crisis makes the point
starkly. We see it in droughts and wild
wildfires, in record-breaking heat, and
in the growing pressure on food, water,
and energy accessibility and security.
The challenge before us is no longer a
lack of solutions. We have the
solutions. We know what's required. Now,
we need to deliver.
Therefore, Cup 31 must be a cup of
implementation, turning ambition into
action and real world results,
delivering out the objectives of the
Paris Agreement and is 1.5° Celsius
temperature goal. With only four years
left to 2030, we must also be honest
about where we stand on sustainable
development goals, both in terms of
achievements and challenges.
Let's make the upcoming SGD summit a
turning point. 2030 must not be a missed
deadline.
Excellencies, this year we'll be
selecting a new Secretary General.
Denmark thanks Secretary General
Gutierrez for a decade of dedicated
service to this organization, often
under exceptionally difficult
circumstances.
The next secretary general will take
over an organization under strain and
under scrutiny.
To bring UN safely into the future, we
must select a person who can work to
restore the global trust in the UN and
among its member states.
Excellencies, in closing, I'm happy to
inform you that last week in this very
building, Denmark, Greenland, and the
United States signed an agreement on
security, which strengthen the defense
of Greenland, the NATO area, and the
American continent.
The agreement is good for Greenland, for
Denmark, for the United States, for NATO
and Europe, and for international peace
and security.
Progress can still be made when we
consult the compass. I thank you.
I thank the chair of delegation of
Denmark.
